evidence_titles: Devtools must be open source (exe.dev)
evidence_summaries: My comment on Devtools must be open source (exe.dev) — Hacker News. One of the arguments for open source software for end-users has always been the freedom to examine and modify how that software works. The reality for most people - even expert programmers - has been that the freedom is more about being able to lean on other people to do that. Most people can't justify the time commitment needed to read and then modify the code for tools they use very often. I think LLMs have changed that equation in a way that makes the original dream much more feasible. Several times a day I'll prompt regular Claude chat to "Clone x/y from GitHub and tell me how Z works". Getting software to compile in order to start hacking on it used to be enough friction that I often wouldn't bother. Now I treat that as a zero time investment challenge: tell Codex or Claude Code to checkout and build X and then come back ten minutes later and see how it got on. I'm not habitually modifying the software I use yet, but I can see a path to that which didn't exist a year or so ago. 2️⃣ Agent-native DX
You can still ship "slow" navs if you want, e.g. by blocking navs on server-side data fetching ala PHP olden days. But even then, your agent will be given *choices*, like setting up a for instant loading shells. Agents also get built-in versioned docs.

This is our best release for agents by far, which will also make your upgrading journey very smooth. I've had an easy time bumping my projects to 16.3 and enabling instant navs, having my agent migrate everything without issues.

And so much more. 16.3 is more cost-efficient to serve, both in self-hosting and serverless environments. Faster to type-check… Thank you to the 90 contributors to this release!

worth_tracking.title: My 6 biggest takeaways from @karan4d, @NousResearch co-founder, on getting the most out of Hermes Agent:
worth_tracking.social_original_text:
My 6 biggest takeaways from @karan4d, @NousResearch co-founder, on getting the most out of Hermes Agent:

1. The “personal” in personal agent is not the model

It’s the agent’s memory of your conversations and the skills you’ve built with it. Karan barely notices when he swaps models because his Hermes already has so much context about him.

2. Try different Hermes personalities

Use /personality to switch response styles. Try “teacher” when learning something new, “concise” when you want crisp answers, and even “kawaii” or “pirate” for fun.

3. Use separate agents to do the work and evaluate it

Karan calls “you’re absolutely right” reward hacking because the model is optimizing for your approval. Have one agent do the work and a fresh agent with no previous context evaluate it independently for errors, weak assumptions, and missing evidence.

4. A self-improving agent needs to clean up after itself

Hermes Curator tracks skill usage, marks inactive skills as stale, and moves long-unused ones into a recoverable archive. This prevents agent-created skills from piling up forever.

5. Intelligence should be a public good

Karan believes people should be able to run Hermes locally or use it with whichever model works best. He worries about a future where only a handful of companies dominate AI and open source gets squeezed out.

6. Go weird and make your childhood dreams come true

Karan uses Hermes to mod Chao Garden, the virtual-pet mode inside Sonic Adventure 2. He asked it to bring a location from Sonic Adventure 1 into the sequel and add features that he’s always wanted since childhood.

📌 Watch the full episode here: https://t.co/3E7IC0TzNr

evidence_titles: Devtools must be open source (exe.dev)
evidence_summaries: My comment on Devtools must be open source (exe.dev) — Hacker News. One of the arguments for open source software for end-users has always been the freedom to examine and modify how that software works. The reality for most people - even expert programmers - has been that the freedom is more about being able to lean on other people to do that. Most people can't justify the time commitment needed to read and then modify the code for tools they use very often. I think LLMs have changed that equation in a way that makes the original dream much more feasible. Several times a day I'll prompt regular Claude chat to "Clone x/y from GitHub and tell me how Z works". Getting software to compile in order to start hacking on it used to be enough friction that I often wouldn't bother. Now I treat that as a zero time investment challenge: tell Codex or Claude Code to checkout and build X and then come back ten minutes later and see how it got on. I'm not habitually modifying the software I use yet, but I can see a path to that which didn't exist a year or so ago. industry_views.title: Next.js 16.3: faster, better, stronger. My highlights:
industry_views.social_original_text:
faster, better, stronger. My highlights:

0️⃣ Faster dev & builds
Shoutout to Fable for improving memory use, and the team for landing the incremental 𝚗𝚎𝚡𝚝 𝚋𝚞𝚒𝚕𝚍 cache.

1️⃣ Instant navigations are 🔥
The people wanted SPAs, they shall get SPAs. By turning on instant navs (which will soon be default), your agent is basically forced to make things fast.

2️⃣ Agent-native DX
You can still ship "slow" navs if you want, e.g. by blocking navs on server-side data fetching ala PHP olden days. But even then, your agent will be given *choices*, like setting up a for instant loading shells. Agents also get built-in versioned docs.

This is our best release for agents by far, which will also make your upgrading journey very smooth. I've had an easy time bumping my projects to 16.3 and enabling instant navs, having my agent migrate everything without issues.

And so much more. 16.3 is more cost-efficient to serve, both in self-hosting and serverless environments. Faster to type-check… Thank you to the 90 contributors to this release!

industry_views.title: My 6 biggest takeaways from @karan4d, @NousResearch co-founder, on getting the most out of Hermes Agent:
industry_views.social_original_text:
My 6 biggest takeaways from @karan4d, @NousResearch co-founder, on getting the most out of Hermes Agent:

1. The “personal” in personal agent is not the model

It’s the agent’s memory of your conversations and the skills you’ve built with it. Karan barely notices when he swaps models because his Hermes already has so much context about him.

2. Try different Hermes personalities

Use /personality to switch response styles. Try “teacher” when learning something new, “concise” when you want crisp answers, and even “kawaii” or “pirate” for fun.

3. Use separate agents to do the work and evaluate it

Karan calls “you’re absolutely right” reward hacking because the model is optimizing for your approval. Have one agent do the work and a fresh agent with no previous context evaluate it independently for errors, weak assumptions, and missing evidence.

4. A self-improving agent needs to clean up after itself

Hermes Curator tracks skill usage, marks inactive skills as stale, and moves long-unused ones into a recoverable archive. This prevents agent-created skills from piling up forever.

5. Intelligence should be a public good

Karan believes people should be able to run Hermes locally or use it with whichever model works best. He worries about a future where only a handful of companies dominate AI and open source gets squeezed out.

6. Go weird and make your childhood dreams come true

Karan uses Hermes to mod Chao Garden, the virtual-pet mode inside Sonic Adventure 2. He asked it to bring a location from Sonic Adventure 1 into the sequel and add features that he’s always wanted since childhood.

📌 Watch the full episode here: https://t.co/3E7IC0TzNr

items.ai_summary: Simon Willison评论认为，LLM使开源软件代码的可检查与可修改自由从理论变为日常可行，他常用Claude和Codex快速克隆仓库并理解代码。
items.brief: Simon Willison评论认为，LLM使开源软件代码的可检查与可修改自由从理论变为日常可行，他常用Claude和Codex快速克隆仓库并理解代码。
evidence_titles: Devtools must be open source (exe.dev)
evidence_summaries: My comment on Devtools must be open source (exe.dev) — Hacker News. One of the arguments for open source software for end-users has always been the freedom to examine and modify how that software works. The reality for most people - even expert programmers - has been that the freedom is more about being able to lean on other people to do that. Most people can't justify the time commitment needed to read and then modify the code for tools they use very often. I think LLMs have changed that equation in a way that makes the original dream much more feasible. Several times a day I'll prompt regular Claude chat to "Clone x/y from GitHub and tell me how Z works". Getting software to compile in order to start hacking on it used to be enough friction that I often wouldn't bother. Now I treat that as a zero time investment challenge: tell Codex or Claude Code to checkout and build X and then come back ten minutes later and see how it got on. I'm not habitually modifying the software I use yet, but I can see a path to that which didn't exist a year or so ago. items.title: Next.js 16.3: faster, better, stronger. My highlights:
items.social_original_text:
faster, better, stronger. My highlights:

0️⃣ Faster dev & builds
Shoutout to Fable for improving memory use, and the team for landing the incremental 𝚗𝚎𝚡𝚝 𝚋𝚞𝚒𝚕𝚍 cache.

1️⃣ Instant navigations are 🔥
The people wanted SPAs, they shall get SPAs. By turning on instant navs (which will soon be default), your agent is basically forced to make things fast.

2️⃣ Agent-native DX
You can still ship "slow" navs if you want, e.g. by blocking navs on server-side data fetching ala PHP olden days. But even then, your agent will be given *choices*, like setting up a for instant loading shells. Agents also get built-in versioned docs.

This is our best release for agents by far, which will also make your upgrading journey very smooth. I've had an easy time bumping my projects to 16.3 and enabling instant navs, having my agent migrate everything without issues.

And so much more. 16.3 is more cost-efficient to serve, both in self-hosting and serverless environments. Faster to type-check… Thank you to the 90 contributors to this release!

items.title: My 6 biggest takeaways from @karan4d, @NousResearch co-founder, on getting the most out of Hermes Agent:
items.social_original_text:
My 6 biggest takeaways from @karan4d, @NousResearch co-founder, on getting the most out of Hermes Agent:

1. The “personal” in personal agent is not the model

It’s the agent’s memory of your conversations and the skills you’ve built with it. Karan barely notices when he swaps models because his Hermes already has so much context about him.

2. Try different Hermes personalities

Use /personality to switch response styles. Try “teacher” when learning something new, “concise” when you want crisp answers, and even “kawaii” or “pirate” for fun.

3. Use separate agents to do the work and evaluate it

Karan calls “you’re absolutely right” reward hacking because the model is optimizing for your approval. Have one agent do the work and a fresh agent with no previous context evaluate it independently for errors, weak assumptions, and missing evidence.

4. A self-improving agent needs to clean up after itself

Hermes Curator tracks skill usage, marks inactive skills as stale, and moves long-unused ones into a recoverable archive. This prevents agent-created skills from piling up forever.

5. Intelligence should be a public good

Karan believes people should be able to run Hermes locally or use it with whichever model works best. He worries about a future where only a handful of companies dominate AI and open source gets squeezed out.

6. Go weird and make your childhood dreams come true

Karan uses Hermes to mod Chao Garden, the virtual-pet mode inside Sonic Adventure 2. He asked it to bring a location from Sonic Adventure 1 into the sequel and add features that he’s always wanted since childhood.

📌 Watch the full episode here: https://t.co/3E7IC0TzNr
